extracted.intended_audience: architects, designers, artists, craftsmen, and patrons interested in Gothic architecture and humane craft principles (Victorian-era critique)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines for creating and evaluating Gothic architecture and related craftwork, emphasizing imperfection, variety, invention-first, humane labor practices, and avoidance of slavish finish or copying. Applies to architects, workmen, and patrons deciding how to value design, execution, and labour organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfection is essential to noble architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: "no architecture can be truly noble which is not imperfect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: (1) great minds work beyond their powers of execution so parts will sometimes fail; (2) imperfection is a sign of life, progress, and change — living things are not rigidly perfect. Conclusion: banishing imperfection destroys expression and vitality; good work will necessarily show flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudeness/savageness (roughness) as a noble element
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudeness or imperfection, where necessary to obtain genuine thought or design, is admirable and often essential to Gothic architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a rough, untaught man's thought is desired, it must be allowed to appear in a rough way; from an educated man prefer graceful expression. Do not silence or check unrefined expression by insisting on polished finish before the thought is obtained. The imperfect is preferable to smoothness that has no invention behind it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changefulness / Variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Changefulness or variety in every feature of the building is a defining element of Gothic: parts should not be absolutely alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perpetual variety in design and execution is the reward of allowing independent operation to workmen. The degree of similarity among parts (e.g., whether all capitals are alike) visibly indicates whether workmen were free or enslaved; variety is artistically valuable and makes architecture 'say new and different things.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow independent operation for inferior workmen (liberate the workman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Workmen must be set free to show their weaknesses with their strengths: "Wherever the workman is utterly enslaved, the parts of the building must of course be absolutely like each other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: look for perpetual change in design/execution to know if laborers were free. Liberty of the labourer ennobles architecture; freedom produces perpetual variety and expression that uniform, enslaved execution cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always seek invention first, then execution
rubrics_metrics.description: "Always look for invention first, and after that, for such execution as will help the invention..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand only such execution as will assist the inventor and that the inventor can provide without painful effort. Do not demand refinement of execution where there is no thought — that is 'slaves' work, unredeemed.' Prefer rough work that realizes a practical purpose over smooth work accomplished merely by patience or sandpaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never encourage manufacture of unnecessary articles lacking invention
rubrics_metrics.description: "Never encourage the manufacture of any article not absolutely necessary, in the production of which Invention has no share."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/anti-pattern: glass beads — mass-produced by mechanical repetition with no thought, producing inhuman, degrading labour ('every young lady who buys glass beads is engaged in the slave-trade'). Contrast: glass cups or vessels that embody invention (form, color, engraving) are defensible purchases because they pay for invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never demand exact finish for its own sake; require finish only for noble/practical ends
rubrics_metrics.description: "Never demand an exact finish for its own sake, but only for some practical or noble end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact finish that does not serve invention or a noble practical purpose degrades workers and produces slaves' work. Finish is desirable when it leads to fuller accomplishment of noble purposes (e.g., masters such as Michelangelo, Turner), but should not be required of lower men who cannot finish consummately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never encourage imitation or copying except to preserve record
rubrics_metrics.description: "Never encourage imitation or copying of any kind, except for the sake of preserving record of great works."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation produces repetition and diminishes invention; architecture (like literature) should 'say new and different things.' Copying is only justified when preserving the record of great works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not turn people into tools — choose between making tools or making men
rubrics_metrics.description: You must "either make a tool of the creature, or a man of him. You cannot make both."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expecting tool-like precision from human beings requires unhumanizing them, giving all their spirit to mechanical precision and wasting their higher faculties. Conversely, making a man of the worker loses engine-turned precision but gains imagination and 'the whole majesty' of the person. Policy choice: prefer human development over mechanical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value manual labor combined with thought; restore dignity to craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual labour should not be despised when governed by intellect; the workman ought often to be thinking, and the thinker often to be working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: painters grind their own colors; architects work in the mason's yard; masters be skilled operatives. Aim to make all professions liberal and to remove the dishonor from manual labour. Combining thought and labor makes both healthy and happy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of division of labor that fragments human life
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern division of labour often divides men themselves into fragments of life, leaving only tiny pieces of intelligence for repetitive tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturing that optimizes for cheapness, convenience, or finish at the cost of forming human spirits is morally and socially degrading. The remedy: public understanding of which kinds of labor are ennobling; sacrifice of some convenience/cheapness; and a demand for products resulting from healthy, ennobling labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize invention and the thoughtful part of workers over flawless execution
rubrics_metrics.description: In hiring or employing people, seek out the thoughtful part of them and prize that, even if it comes with faults: 'look for the thoughtful part of them, and get that out of them, whatever we lose for it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can teach mechanical precision, but you cannot make a man think for another. Encourage and allow thinking in laborers even though it produces hesitation, errors, and roughness — these are the signs of a 'man' rather than a mere machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicate finish is legitimate when used by great masters to serve noble purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicate finish is desirable from the greatest masters and is given by them when it leads to fuller accomplishment of noble purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Michelangelo, Leonardo, Phidias, Perugino, Turner — they finished with exquisite care when finish served invention. The rule: allow finish where it genuinely helps the invention; otherwise prefer invention-first. Finish without thought is mere slaves' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture (and art) should be inventive and entertaining, not merely orderly repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Great art, whether in words, colors, or stones, 'does not say the same thing over and over again'; merit consists in saying new and different things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Love of order and correctness serves practical life but is not the same as love of art. Do not mistake repetitive 'proper forms' for artistic merit; require architects to be not only correct but also inventive and entertaining, as you would a novelist.
